subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: A Ruler for How Real a Technology Actually Is
lesson.summary: Technology readiness levels are a simple nine point scale, originally developed by NASA, for describing how far a technology has progressed from a basic scientific idea to a proven, operational product.
lesson.body:
Technology readiness levels, abbreviated TRL, are a 1 to 9 scale that NASA developed in the 1970s to answer a deceptively simple practical question: when an engineer says a technology is ready, ready for what, exactly? One engineer's confident it works might mean a promising result observed once on a lab bench, while another's might mean hardware that has already flown successfully in space. Those are very different levels of maturity, and confusing them caused real, expensive problems, including project failures when a technology only proven in a controlled laboratory setting was assumed to be ready for use in an actual spacecraft. TRL gave engineers, managers, and outside reviewers a shared vocabulary, so a readiness claim could be checked against a specific, defined level instead of simply taken on faith or inferred from confident language.

The scale runs from TRL 1, basic principles observed, meaning a research paper describes an underlying physical phenomenon with no engineering application yet in view, through a series of middle levels where a technology is tested first in a laboratory and then in conditions increasingly resembling the real world, up to TRL 9, proven through successful operation in its actual, final application. TRL 6, a rough and commonly cited midpoint, typically means a full prototype has been demonstrated in a relevant environment, not just a lab bench, but not yet the final operational setting either. Exact wording varies slightly across NASA, the Department of Defense, the European Space Agency, and other organizations that have each adapted the original scale for their own purposes, but the underlying nine step structure and its logic stay consistent across all of them.

TRL matters well beyond aerospace and defense because it lets outsiders, investors, journalists, policymakers among them, translate an exciting technical claim into a concrete, checkable maturity estimate without needing deep domain expertise themselves. A drug still in preclinical testing sits in a very different risk category than one that has already finished a phase 3 clinical trial, and TRL captures an analogous distinction for hardware and physical technologies: a laboratory demonstration and a deployed, operational product are simply not the same category of achievement, even when press coverage or a company's own marketing describes both using similarly confident, forward looking language.

For a technology as complex and unfamiliar to most people as quantum computing, having a standardized, external way to ask how mature is this, really, is especially valuable, since the underlying physics is hard enough that most observers, including most professional investors, cannot independently verify a specific technical claim on its merits. The next concept walks through what each of the nine levels concretely means in practice, and the one after that applies the scale directly to where quantum computing hardware actually sits today.
